title: Routines: why are they important and how can we embed them? embed-them/
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino prepares a CPD session on classroom routines, drawing on Tom Bennett's Running the Room, the Michaela staff's The Power of Culture and Lemov's Teach Like a Champion 2.0. She argues that expectations must be explicitly taught, modelled and maintained rather than merely announced, and describes her own SLANT routine for listening. The post then works through routines for questioning, including Cold Call, mini-whiteboard procedures, choral response and Think-Pair-Share, each with specific cues and steps. She also covers modelling through worked examples, and routines for discussion that keep everyone tracking the speaker. Her summary of embedding routines is to narrate the positive, describe and show, stay consistent and explain the why to students. The thesis is that investing in routines saves time that can be spent on teaching.
points: Expectations should be taught and modelled, not just stated, and then maintained constantly.
Narrating the positive by naming students who follow a routine quickly pulls others into line.
Cold Call works as a routine for sharing knowledge when it is used consistently and without ridicule, giving a second chance to a student who did not know the answer.
Mini-whiteboards, choral response and Think-Pair-Share only work when each has a precise, repeated cue and set of steps.
Consistency is the key to routines, and explaining their purpose to students helps them see how routines create more learning time.
quotes: He argues that we must teach rather than just tell our students about the routines we expect them to follow. And then, importantly, we need to be consistent and always remind students of the routines through constant maintenance.

Narrate The Positive by pointing out students who are demonstrating an expectation perfectly. The difference this makes is significant- as soon as you praise or acknowledge Student A who has started writing, Student B who was hitherto taken too long to get their book out of their bag, will speed up to catch up.

Some people (including students) think Cold Call is a way to catch a student out. But if used routinely, it should be obvious that it really is a way for the class to share what they know. If they don’t know an answer, it can serve as a learning opportunity without any danger of being ridiculed.
Choral response has become a bit of a revelation. I resisted using it for such a long time and finally gave it a go.
It is important that students are actually given sufficient time to think. Get students to write down their thoughts to the question you have posed so they can better develop their thinking.
Consistency: this is absolutely key to embed effective routines. You need to be consistent all the time or students will stop following your routines

Good routines can make a lesson run smoothly and allow you to focus on teaching and modelling. It does take time to embed them fully into lessons but if you are consistent and persistent with them, eventually a lot of time is saved, which can be used for far more important things.
